newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma still holding people after unrest-Suu Kyi.
newsitem.headline: Burma still holding people after unrest-Suu Kyi.

text.p: Burmese opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi said on Monday the military government still held 105 people after December's student protests.

A senior member of the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) told Reuters in an interview the ruling council was still holding some detainees but did not say whether they were arrested in connection with the December protests.
He also said the SLORC had no plans to hold dialogue with her, saying she was implacably against the military council.
"She will always be against us...at this time, it is impossible (to hold dialogue with her)," Lieutenant General Kyaw Ba, a founding member of the SLORC and hotels and tourism minister, said.
Suu Kyi told a news conference those detained included 24 students, 34 members and supporters of her National League for Democracy Party (NLD), 18 NLD youth and 29 non-NLD members.
On Saturday a SLORC spokesman said none were still held.
Students led several weeks of street protests late last year, the worst since soldiers crushed mass pro-democracy demonstrations in 1988.
Suu Kyi also criticised government statements that public access to her would be blocked until her personal safety situation improved and said she did not need their security.
"I have said so, there is no need to take care of my security," she said.

Suu Kyi has been at the forefront of Burma's pro-democracy movement since 1988 despite being under house arrest between 1989 and 1995. Her NLD won a landslide election victory in 1990 although the result has not been recognised by the SLORC.

She angered ruling generals by pulling her NLD out of the convention in November 1995. Western powers, led by the United States, want the SLORC to engage in a dialogue with Suu Kyi, to settle political differences.

Without giving a time frame for when the SLORC hoped to have a new constituion written, the SLORC's Kyaw Ba said greater unity had to be fostered with a host of autonomy-seeking ethnic groups before the army could devise a way to share power.
Suu Kyi condemned closed trials and lack of access to defence counsel for NLD members and others held by the SLORC.
"They should not be afraid to allow defendants to have counsel if they had evidence against them that is solid," she said.
The Nobel laureate also repeated calls to foreign investors to shun Burma until freedom and democracy were restored and because it engaged in "crony capitalism" and hard-liners.
"We think there should be no investments in a country where there is no rule of the law," she added.
Suu Kyi also questioned why the Japanese government had not engaged as much with the Burmese opposition as with the SLORC.

Asked about the current stalemate over dialogue between her and the SLORC, she said she could not accept as a genuine body the SLORC-organised National Convention, which has been drawing up a new constitution for the country.

Suu Kyi, in response to a question at her news conference about whether the SLORC may be divided over the handling of certain issues, had speculated that there were bound to be some in the ruling body who were more pragmatic than others.
"There are 20 members of SLORC. You can't expect 20 people to think in the same way. Some are bound to be more pragmatic than others," she said.
Kyaw Ba denied there was a split within the SLORC and said those who speculated as such were spreading misinformation.
"We don't have anything like that. We are united. If we have differences, we can be easily destroyed by others," he added.
